posts.title: Team agentification
posts.excerpt: Here I have 10 levels of sophistication that a team goes through towards supreme agentification.
posts.content_html:
Team Agentification

eons ago I'd been using ChatGPT for a while to make code snippets for me and I'd be painstakingly copying the output into my terminal, into vim, and then compiling or running my program. When I got an error I would paste that back into ChatGPT and await the correction. The usual development loop, just with AI webchat giving you the answers instead of google and stack overflow, or in fact, having to think for yourself. After doing this for quite a while I took the next step to improve my development process. This was to tighten that loop considerably by moving to a terminal-based AI chatbot which could directly manipulate the filesystem of my git worktree. I began using Codex.

Give yourself some time recall that first moment when you began to use an LLM with all the trappings needed to interface directly on your filesystem. What was the git worktree you first used it in anger against? Do you remember the wonder and realisation your felt that you were at the start of something new? Whether it was Codex, or Claude Code, or Opencode etc. it doesn't matter. We can all share in the discovery of a profound change to the way we do our work. And since you had that moment, the terminal or IDE-based coding assistants have carried on improving. Depending on your standards, and I reckon a majority will agree, notably they became became kind of quite good around mid-2025. Look: don't worry if you feel like you joined the game late, you aren't really that much behind. Early adopters of these agents (and by 'agent' I mean a program that runs a reason-act-observe loop around a language model) weren't really getting stuff done a lot faster than a good software engineer using a web chatbot interface, or to be honest, a good software engineer who knows what they're doing. Software engineers have enjoyed productivity gains from other things prior to AI code generation: google, stack overflow, intellisense, improvements to compiler error reporting, continuous integration jobs. As well as good discipline. One is a fool to neglect non-AI techniques.

Getting back to my own experience: once I'd covered some initial ground with Codex, I looked at my own team at Oxford Nanopore. Everyone was using a web chat like ChatGPT or similar to assist with coding, so that was a great start. But I wanted them to move faster and benefit from the next level of tooling. So as a manager ought to do regularly, I went around each team member individually. Essentially checking that they each had a corporate ChatGPT account, and then ensured they were setup with Codex. I went further. I went around more teams and developers in the company ensuring the same. I checked every developer had a license, negotiating with IT if it was missing. I researched compatibility with each IDE being used and then wrote a company wiki guide for setup, with screenshots as needed, covering all errors and edge cases. I kept pushing, checking people had moved forwards. It took a while to do all this, but having seen the leverage gained, from the tightening of the development loop, I was confident the effort I was making, to get people using Codex earlier than they would have come to it naturally, would have impact.

And so it got me thinking. What's the next step? After you are using a coding agent that works directly on your filesystem, what's next? So I started building an automated code reviewer tool that you could kick off on a CI pipeline, and it would code review the merge request it was on. This is something that operates outside that developer loop. Another tool I thought was needed was a recipes project for integrating with our various company systems. The aim was to give a coding assistant a >99% chance of success at integrating something on the first try, simply because it had a playbook it could follow to get it right. This is something that is purely provisioned for agents, not users. What I'm talking about here is something prior to, but similar to the agent skills framework that Anthropic dropped in October last year. It is such an obvious thing to want to do though: to created precanned directions for an agent. But it takes effort to produce a useful recipe of this kind within an organisation. You have a prerequisite of clear instructions for how to do something manually, in other words that someone else in your company has taken the time and effort to try doing the thing for real and then write up the how-to, and that includes dealing with gotchas and documenting troubleshooting steps (and checking that those actually work). There are no shortcuts to have an AI just do stuff magically: it needs good and complete context to work from if you want that high first-pass success rate.

Accepting that there has to be pre-existing processes and discipline as foundation, it became clear to me that each project I built, or that I inspired a colleague to build (and inspiration is mutual when everyone is going for it), was a stepping stone to something bigger, a not-so-distant future where developers are in symbiosis with agents, rapidly building, fixing and debugging, disrupting the way software is written and resourced at the company. Indeed some other companies are working like this already, though not many.

Looking back I realised that what I had done, pushing the developers in an organisation from ChatGPT to terminal-based agents was a significant part of a clear concrete transition from one kind of level to another. The tools I had been building, and the tools that others were inspired to build, assuming internal adoption and integration, were to form a critical mass leading to another transition. Thus, not long ago I hatched a plan to map out some well-defined stages or levels one had to work through for a team to become progressively more agent-enabled. And so I began work on a progression ladder project. Whilst creating it I've seen a few other lists of stages or ladders in various places , but I have yet to see one that goes into much depth.

Personally I've found competency matrices or progression ladders to be rather dull and dry things. Which is a shame because the point of them is to spark a conversation with those on a quest to make progress along them. I like to do something a bit different and make them a little bit interactive and eye-catching. I've got pictures from ChatGPT, albeit in need of denoising and anomaly correction, to add some inspiration and decoration. I'd have preferred not to push push easily-created AI-generated illustrations on people, in a similar veign to how I don't wish to lure you into my site and then just hand you an AI-generated blog post (this prose is all hand-typed: my promise for my blog posts.). But the guidance I want to deliver with this project is something I want to deliver now, at the start of 2026. Getting out my easel and oil paints will have to wait.

And so let me present to you:

Team Agentification Journey

Here I have 10 levels of sophistication that a team goes through towards supreme agentification. In creating these 10 levels I didn't want to disregard the foundational steps and progress teams make in their engineering culture, discipline and tooling regardless of AI. Indeed the excellent work that software engineers have been doing for decades to raise the game of their teams. So I have allowed for levels 1, 2 and 3 to cover that that. It's important, as if you don't actually progress from level 1 in a natural way, if you don't engage with the discipline and classical automation (not literally classical automation) of levels 2 and 3, but instead skip straight to using agents, then you'll be on level 4 and onwards only superficially. Your team will be operating with advanced tools, but without the foundation to get the most out of them, yet with all the expense. You'll be in the realm of rapid building of technical debt and all the other things people warn about when using an AI tool to code without the required understanding of how to build software and run a software team. In general there are implications for moving onwards to techniques and tools at higher levels without having properly addressed earlier levels. For example, it's inefficient to build delegation without the interfaces that become roads for proper agency, and it's hard to achieve true co-evolution without memory, without a lasting curated team history. Plenty more philosophy I can share another time. I'll now let the journey page speak for itself.

Please take some time to explore! If you have any questions/suggestions, or if you indeed find this infographical ladder useful as a compass, a reminder, or as a vision then please message me. It would be great to hear your story.

posts.author: Ben Huckvale

posts.title: A new TUI and MCP tool: Git Maestro
posts.excerpt: I simply wanted a wrapper around git
posts.content_html:
At least one cultural reference per blog post. That's what I've said to myself.

I couldn't think of anywhere else in the article to put one that was natural, so this is a bit tenuous and forced: Despite the term 'Maestro' this article is about new software, not "some kind of new music" from 0b1111111 years ago. Both because I've created some new software, but also because the new software I've created has features to help you make new software projects. Scott Joplin's own music genre that he spent his life carving out, is a blend of classical techniques and the traits that seeded the jazz movement. So moreover, my feeling is that although the software engineering profession is now in a new kind of epoch there is very much a niche, more than a niche really, for a strong blend of manual, classically-automated and AI-assisted techniques. More on my music tastes another time. Let's talk about this new tool that is in the spirit of that blend.

Whilst at Oxford Nanopore, I came up with a convenience tool project that I thought I would get Codex to build, and I gave it what I thought was a throwaway name: gitlab-maestro. I simply wanted a wrapper around git, that would allow me to quickly create and get a project uploaded to a group on the enterprise gitlab instance. Really just a glorified python script, a convenience tool that can be launched directly from a terminal shell, providing a Text-based User Interface (TUI).

But since I left, I've not stopped building software and so I have still found I needed a similar kind of tool. This is because terminal-based coding agents allow for the transformation of ideas into actual working prototypes with reckless abandon so one is creating projects from scratch far more often than before.

With Claude Code this time, I recreated the same concept again from scratch but for github and called it Git Maestro. Yet after I'd got a working minimal project I thought, well why not have it support each repository vendor so I went back to working on Gitlab, and I thought well I might as well support Azure Devops too! Then users of the library can get developing projects for all these places in double-quick time.

One might have been worried that Github's going to be overwhelmed with a cacophony of new projects as a result of AI-based coding, except it's one of those things that doesn't make big news simply because Microsoft has this all in hand.

For those who don't know btw, Gitlab is absolutely fantastic, and in my opinion is the strongest base foundation on the market on which you can build high quality engineered automated workflows for software development, model training and assessment, and other business processes. Largely because of support for compliance and the self-hosting of runners with your own spec (tons of RAM, high-spec GPUs etc.) which you can connect to your own hardware products that you're developing, and to company systems within the corporate network.

Anyway. Let's get back to how I've designed Git Maestro and what it can do.

Its architecture is defined around a principle that a useful program is one that observes the repo, and then presents various actions based on that observed state in order to assist making genuine progress with the maturity of that repository. Let's give you an example, indeed the first critical observation to make. If a given directory has within it another directory called .git/, or if a parent directory has such a .git directory in it, that then indicates the directory is a git repo (because that's the hidden directory git makes in which to store repo history). But if:

  • .git/ doesn't exist
  • ../.git/ doesn't exist
  • ../../.git/ doesn't exist
  • etc.

then it means the directory is not a repo yet, so could potentially be turned into a git repo. In that case the action to present is one to run git init, and then after that, other actions are needed to set up a default branch, and then add an initial commit. Another thing the program should do is check to see if a remote url is setup in the .git/config file. If not then an action to present to the user is one that offers to create a project on a remote system such as github, which can be done automatically if an API token is available with which it can authenticate. Convenience tools are not useful if they force you to do something i.e. just push all your commits to the new project. So it doesn't force you it: it offers a full push but also other options to push some or no commits.

So these were the first things I implemented. But because I'm a test-driven development nutcase and absolutely love continuous integration, the next feature I wanted, after project creation, was to be able to get the CI/CD pipeline status. Because a common development workflow is to write a feature, write the tests, add a CI/CD workflow (github actions, or gitlab-ci yaml or azure pipelines yaml, and then push up the code and then check that those tests pass on the remote runner and if not go back and edit the tests. Because even if tests run on your own machine, they might not work on the runner (or other people's machines).

But in order to do that check I don't want to have to open the browser page at all to look at the relevant vendor site to see these CI/CD results. I don't want to have to click on the github project, and browse to actions, and look up the failed pipeline, and click on that and scroll down to the error in the job trace. Here is a rule of thumb: if you have to view a browser page whilst developing, then you're missing a script that can do it for you.

Thus getting git-maestro to do that job for me swiftly via some interactive menus without leaving the terminal and having to point and click in the browser was an important milestone. And why not add that capability for each of Github, Azure and Gitlab and support all you lovely open-source and enterprise users?

But I'm not really intending always to do that development workflow myself. It will frequently be what I want a command line AI coding agent to do. Which means Git-maestro needs to be available to such an agent via the Model Context Protocol, whilst still providing the Text-based User Interface for when I want to do it directly.

The three major repository hosting and devops vendors I've been talking about each already provide their own MCP server projects for using their APIs:

  • Github MCP Server
  • Gitlab MCP Server
  • Azure MCP Server

These each give access to a rich API, and in theory your agent could autonomously complete a project for you on that system using the required MCP server. Indeed each agent could use these but also, for example on github, the agent could directly call say gh, the github cli tool if the user has that installed. If you watch, say, Claude code doing something complex with github it will call one gh command after another to reach its goal.

You may then ask, why develop another MCP that does a similar thing? Well as mentioned, I want Git Maestro to be a TUI as well, which these aren't: because I'm interested in making tools that use AI but also mean I don't have to rely on AI. Also with these MCPs, is the agent going to be able to do the job efficiently? With Git Maestro I'm looking to solve certain problems that speed up my own particular workflow. It's not intended to be a blanket tool covering all possible tasks you'd want to facilitate an agent to do for you. So the MCP surface is targetted, and if I can help it, more reliable and more token efficient than using these general MCP servers to achieve certain tasks. I've got no stats to prove this yet, mind.

In summary, why use Git Maestro?

Well:

  1. It's a TUI tool as well as an MCP, so you can use it from the command line as a user (costing zero tokens) as well as allowing an agent to use it.
  2. It combines some (not all) of the functions needed for interacting with all of these major DevOps vendors, rather than just focusing on one of them.
  3. It wraps up certain git workflows to make things a bit easier and faster.

I've got more things I'd like this thing to be able to do such as managing the stash, hunk staging, and wrapping tasks that involve: filter-branch (AKA laying waste to repo history). Most likely I'll add these when I personally need them. But I will welcome contributions wholeheartedly. If anyone else cares to give this tool a spin and you like it and then you think of something you'd like it to do, please add it and make a pull request. The temptation to build new projects that do something similar is high, because it is so easy to ask a coding assistant to do it for you I know. Still, if you can get past that, I would enjoy having a little company building this project into a trusted, rich and powerful tool to wrap git functionality.

Git Maestro, take it away!

agent could directly call say [gh, the github cli
tool](https://cli.github.com/) if the user has that installed. If you watch,
say, Claude code doing something complex with github it will call
one `gh` command after another to reach its goal.

You may then ask, why develop another MCP that does a similar thing?  Well as
mentioned, I want Git Maestro to be a TUI as well, which these aren't: because
I'm interested in making tools that use AI but also mean I don't have to rely
on AI. Also with these MCPs, is the agent going to be able to do the job
efficiently? With Git Maestro I'm looking to solve certain problems that speed
up my own particular workflow.  It's not intended to be a blanket tool covering
all possible tasks you'd want to facilitate an agent to do for you. So the MCP
surface is targetted, and if I can help it, more reliable and more token
efficient than using these general MCP servers to achieve certain tasks. I've
got no stats to prove this yet, mind.

In summary, why use Git Maestro?

Well:
1. It's a TUI tool as well as an MCP, so you can use it from the command line
as a user (costing zero tokens) as well as allowing an agent to use it.
2. It combines some (not all) of the functions needed for interacting with all
of these major DevOps vendors, rather than just focusing on one of them. 
3. It wraps up certain git workflows to make things a bit easier and faster.

I've got more things I'd like this thing to be able to do such as
[managing the stash](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-stash),
[hunk staging](https://git-scm.com/book/en/v2/Git-Tools-Interactive-Staging),
and wrapping tasks that involve:
[filter-branch](https://git-scm.com/docs/git-filter-branch) (AKA laying
waste to repo history). Most likely I'll add these when I personally need them.
But I will welcome contributions wholeheartedly. If anyone else cares to give
this tool a spin and you like it and then you think of something you'd like it
to do, please add it and make a pull request. The temptation to build new
projects that do something similar is high, because it is so easy to ask a
coding assistant to do it for you I know. Still, if you can get past that, I
would enjoy having a little company building this project into a trusted, rich
and powerful tool to wrap git functionality.

[Git Maestro](https://github.com/benhuckvale/git-maestro/), take it away!

posts.title: Welcome to My Blog
posts.excerpt: An introduction to this blog and what you can expect to find here.
posts.content_html:
I've built a portfolio site, with profile and blog posts. Finally!

It took a while to get to this point, because "One does not simply make a portfolio site" if one is a software engineer, because the site itself has to be constructed in a software-engineering-ish way. It's like, if you live on a street with an electrician who would you expect to have the best Christmas lights? So I can't let myself down and plump for Wix.

So what does that entail? Well I normalised out the dependencies, and built a CI/CD pipeline (Github actions) that will process my content to build the site. I have a repository with a toolkit to create various formats of my personal career and portfolio data, a repo that actually has my career data in it which uses that toolkit to export the data for the site, and a website repo that uses that data to build the site, and deploy it. This might seem like overkill, but I also use the same arrangement to build my resume, and to provide my linked-in profile content (I just haven't dared write a playwright bot for linked-in that will edit it into the site for me, as it's sort of against their terms of service, maybe).

Regarding the profile part of the site, I wanted to be able to highlight elements of my resume when you select a skill. So you'll see that's what it does (at least at the time of writing). It doesn't do this with a semantic lookup with embeddings, which is what I thought I'd do initially. It's presently keyword-driven which is a pragmatic choice. It uses tailwind for styling and I'll admit, I never looked at the tailwind site and didn't see their commercial plans, because I simply asked the coding assistant to use it without thinking about the impact of AI on tailwind.

Regarding this blog, after faffing around with headless content management systems and various site building frameworks I just settled on a bespoke project to handle my content and a custom React renderer to present it. The reason I didn't go for a CMS approach (like Sanity or Payload) is because actually I do not want my blog posts in a database because that sits outside git version control, and because I don't want to use a format to store them like JSON which is hard to edit by hand. The reason I didn't go for an existing website framework like Astro or Gatsby (and I did try using these) is because frankly it's too easy simply to instruct Claude Code to build a custom setup and do everything exactly the way I want to do it with React. Having said that I admire the choice of the name Gatsby.

Anyway, what will you find here in this blog? A while ago I thought that if I had a blog I would routinely post to it so that I always alternate between hard and soft topics. So let's try that now that I have one. People use the term soft skills to refer to supposedly non-technical things like coaching and people management and politics and leadership, but these are are in fact hard, and profoundly technical in their own way. Still, we'll go with that as a means of division, although the criteria I use to make hard placement of an article one side or the other will certainly be soft. Since this introductory post is classified as soft, it'll be hard next time.

I'll be writing about various topics related to:

  • 🧱 Software engineering and architecture
  • 🧱 Web development (Python, JavaScript, React)
  • 🧱 DevOps and automation
  • 🧱 Project showcases and experiments
  • 🪶 Career development in tech
  • 🪶 Management
  • 🪶 Leadership
  • 🪶 Industry Comment

Regarding whether an AI is going to help me write this or not, what I'll promise you is that (unless there is a reason to and I'll make it very clear) I'll be writing the prose for my own posts from scratch to polish without help, though I may have an AI fact check, write code, add links, add images or format stuff. This means if for some reason my humble writings actually are of interest to you, you will definitely get my ugly unguarded, extremely edgy and dynamically delusional opinion without the smug smoothing of the painfully polished AI tone, embossed with em-dashes or otherwise. It'll be like a craft beer, but worse since I've never brewed beer before. Still, if it's not like anything else you've tasted and so for some reason you keep coming back I'll be very happy.
